<tr><td>

[KeyPolicyError](./runtime.keypolicyerror.md)

</td><td>

Thrown when a stored per-key policy cannot be read back as a valid policy document.

Surfaced rather than swallowed: silently dropping an unreadable key policy would fall back to the host policy alone, which is \*wider\* than what the operator declared for that key. A key policy that cannot be read is a hard error, and callers fail the request closed.

</td></tr>

</td><td>

Error thrown when a requested permission is well-formed but differs only in letter case from a permission the app defines. Resolution order: 1. The `MACTS_HOME` environment variable, when set to a non-empty, non-whitespace value (custom installations). 2. `~/.macts`<!-- -->, where the home directory comes from `os.homedir()`<!-- -->.

An empty or whitespace-only `MACTS_HOME` is treated as \*\*unset\*\* and the default `~/.macts` is used instead. This prevents a set-but-empty variable from producing a cwd-relative path for the signing secret and key database.

`os.homedir()` is used deliberately instead of `process.env['HOME']`<!-- -->: it is platform-correct and never returns an empty string or the literal `~` when `HOME` is unset (e.g. cron, containers, CI, some service managers). Using `process.env['HOME'] ?? <tr><td>

[resolveGovernanceForRequest(governance, apiKeyId)](./runtime.resolvegovernanceforrequest.md)

</td><td>

Resolve the governance context for a single call from the authenticated API key.

This is the per-caller half of governance resolution. It is a named, shared seam because "which policy applies to this caller" must be answered the same way by every surface that enforces governance.

The whole context is carried through, not just the policy, so an approval gate configured on the surface reaches the call untouched.

A resolver failure propagates to the caller, which must fail the call closed: an unreadable key policy is \*not\* the same as no key policy, and treating it as such would silently widen the boundary back to the host policy.

</td></tr>

<tr><td>

[validateApiKey(token)](./runtime.validateapikey.md)

</td><td>

Validate an API key token.

Checks: 1. Token format (must start with macts_sk\_) 2. JWT signature 3. Expiration (if set) 4. Payload structure 5. Stored record: the key store must hold an unrevoked record for the key. A signature alone never makes a key valid; a key with no stored record (deleted, or never stored) fails with `UNKNOWN_KEY`<!-- -->, and a revoked one with `REVOKED`<!-- -->.

The stored status is cached per process for at most five seconds. Revoking or deleting a key through this process's key store drops its cached status, so the next validation here sees the change at once. A change made by another process (for example the CLI, while a server runs) is seen here once the cached status expires, within five seconds. A missing record is never cached.

</td></tr>

<tr><td>

</td><td>

Governance state for a deployment that seeks human approval.

The audit writer is \*\*required\*\* on this arm. Seeking a human decision and then having nowhere to record it would let a `confirm-first` operation execute with no attributable trace of who permitted it — so that combination is made unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.

</td></tr>
<tr><td>

[GovernanceContextWithoutApprovals](./runtime.governancecontextwithoutapprovals.md)

</td><td>

Governance state for a deployment with \*\*no\*\* approval channel configured.

`confirm-first` calls are withheld and reported as pending. The audit writer is optional here: enforcement still runs without one, it just persists nothing.

</td></tr>
<tr><td>

[KeyMetadataUpdate](./runtime.keymetadataupdate.md)

</td><td>

The fields of a stored key record that may change after the key is issued.

Only the display name. A key's permissions and expiry are carried by its signed token and fixed when it is issued; the stored record is the receipt of that grant, so the grant cannot be edited. To narrow what a key may do, set its policy with [setKeyPolicy()](./runtime.setkeypolicy.md)<!-- -->. To change its grant, revoke it with [revokeKey()](./runtime.revokekey.md) and issue a new one.

Every other `ApiKeyMetadata` field is declared as `never`<!-- -->, derived from `ApiKeyMetadata` itself, so a value that carries one is a type error even when it is not a fresh object literal (a variable holding `{ name, permissions }`<!-- -->, or a `Partial<ApiKeyMetadata>`<!-- -->), and a field added to `ApiKeyMetadata` later is refused the same way.

</td></tr>
<tr><td>

[KeyPolicyResolver](./runtime.keypolicyresolver.md)

</td><td>

Resolves the governance policy attached to an API key, per request.

Implementations must return `undefined` — never a permissive placeholder policy — when a key has no policy of its own, so the caller can apply the host policy alone and preserve pre-per-key behavior exactly.

</td></tr>

## Variables

<table><thead><tr><th>

Variable

</th><th>

Description

</th></tr></thead>
<tbody><tr><td>

[ALLOW_ALL_POLICY](./runtime.allow_all_policy.md)

</td><td>

The allow-all policy used when no policy file is configured.

`defaultDisposition: 'allowed'` + an empty `apps` list means every capability is permitted, preserving pre-governance behavior. Deep-frozen (including the nested `apps` / `tags` arrays) so this shared constant cannot be mutated by a consumer — a shallow `Object.freeze` would leave those arrays writable.

</td></tr>
<tr><td>

[DEFAULT_KEY_POLICY_CACHE_TTL_MS](./runtime.default_key_policy_cache_ttl_ms.md)

</td><td>

Default lifetime of a cached per-key policy.

Short on purpose: a policy edit is a security-relevant change, and an operator tightening a key's policy should not have to wait long (or restart the server) for it to bite. [KeyPolicyResolver.invalidate()](./runtime.keypolicyresolver.invalidate.md) makes it immediate.

</td></tr>
<tr><td>

[RESERVED_APP_ROUTE_SEGMENTS](./runtime.reserved_app_route_segments.md)

</td><td>

Names that can never be an app's route segment.

</td></tr>
</tbody></table>
